Research software

klue
R package · GitHub · R-universe
An R package implementing the specification rule for latent class logit models from the companion paper. It estimates latent class models from clustering-based starting values, fits the mixed logit benchmark, and reports BIC, AIC, ICL, and entropy diagnostics.

title: Software
text:
Side projects
Yalla and Clue are free and work offline, with your data stored on the device. Signing in is optional and syncs your data across devices. Both are plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript without a build step and install on the iPhone home screen as progressive web apps.

Yalla
Offline-first workout tracker · App · GitHub






NoteMore





It tracks training volume across twelve muscle groups, shown as a balance radar, and suggests deload weeks from cumulative load. It builds plans around your venue (home, park, gym) and logged injuries. Volume for bodyweight exercises counts body weight plus any added weight.





Clue
Knowledge and debate trainer · App · GitHub






NoteMore





New cards turn up in a discovery feed and open in layers, starting with the gist. A simplified SM-2 spaced-repetition schedule brings cards back for review. A map of what you know grows as you learn and shows cards due for review as faded nodes. Every card cites sources from an evidence registry, which records the strength of evidence for each source.





Mäander
Bike routing for quiet, nature-oriented rides in Germany






NoteMore





Mäander (TypeScript, MapLibre, BRouter) uses a custom routing profile that favours parks and forests and avoids busy roads. Motorways carry a 700 m noise halo, and forest tracks cost a fraction of paved roads. One slider moves a route from fastest to greenest. It also plans round trips of a chosen length and compass direction and compares several route alternatives side by side.

title: Research
text:
Working papers

Classes or Continuum? A Pre-Registrable Specification Rule for Latent Class Logit Models
Companion R package: klue






NoteAbstract





Latent class multinomial logit (LCMNL) models describe preference heterogeneity as a finite number of classes, mixed multinomial logit (MMNL) models as a continuous mixing distribution. Fitting an LCMNL requires three choices: starting values for a likelihood with many local maxima, the number of classes, and whether classes fit better than a continuous distribution. This paper proposes a pre-registrable rule for all three: starting values from clustering respondents by their choices, the number of classes by BIC with an entropy check on the certainty of class assignment, and an MMNL benchmark that reads preference heterogeneity as continuous when its BIC is at least six points lower. A Monte Carlo study evaluates the rule under a blocked D-efficient design, as used in practice, and an idealised randomised design. Under the blocked design the clustering starts reach the highest log-likelihood found more often than starts from the pooled MNL or random partitions, and about as often as Apollo’s default search, in 2–3 seconds against 38–78 minutes; under the randomised design the clustering and pooled-MNL starts reach it equally often. BIC selects the true number of classes in 94.5% of blocked-design conditions. The benchmark picks the LCMNL in 63 of 64 discrete conditions and never when preferences are continuous, even where BIC alone finds spurious classes. On five public stated-choice datasets the MMNL has the lowest BIC on the four from real respondents and ties on the synthetic one.





Two Countries, One Divide: Fear of Climate Change Splits Support for Forest Conservation
with Jens Abildtrup, David W. Shanafelt, Antonello Lobianco, and Harald Vacik · Highly Commended Paper Award, 8th Workshop on Non-Market Valuation (Leeds, 2024)






NoteAbstract





Who would pay for forest conservation, and why? Public programmes depend on the answer, yet studies report average willingness to pay, which hides the divides beneath it, and opinions on climate change have become politically polarised. Discrete choice experiments in Austria (N = 595) and France (N = 1,874) value publicly funded programmes that restore damaged private forests with climate-adapted stands. We model preference heterogeneity with a stated selection rule and report every model we estimate. The same divide appears in both countries: three quarters of respondents support the programmes, one quarter mostly declines to pay. Fear of climate change draws the line, most sharply in Austria; whether people believe that climate change can still be stopped makes no difference. Supporters would pay three to four times as much as the reluctant for climate-adapted forests, similar amounts in both countries, and in Austria amounts of the order of the planting costs. Climate concern divides public support for forest conservation; local party politics does not.





Audited Alike, Valued Alike? Household Preferences for Public or Private Delivery of EU and Tropical Forest Carbon
Choice experiment pre-registered on OSF for France, Germany and Denmark · Five French pilot rounds






NoteAbstract





To close its projected 2030 shortfall in land-sector removals, the EU can buy forest tonnes at home or abroad, from public or private providers, or cut emissions at source. With quality fixed by audit, I estimate how much households value who delivers a tonne and where and, from the same choices, how much weight they give climate damage that falls on others. In five exploratory French pilot rounds of a choice experiment pre-registered for France, Germany and Denmark, households were willing to pay slightly more for public than for private delivery in the EU, more for EU than for tropical forests and far more for a forest programme than for cutting emissions at source. Shown their household’s share of the worldwide damage, they gave this harm to others less weight than their own money, below the full weight that appraisal at a global social cost of carbon gives it. For the review of the EU’s removal certification and for the 2040 target, private delivery and tropical credits thus draw less support than public removals in the EU, and forest removals more than cuts at source.





The Net Climate Value of Carbon Credits: Pricing Leakage, Time, and Reversal
with Jens Abildtrup, Philippe Delacote, Andreas Kontoleon, Ben Filewod, Hannes Böttcher, Tommaso Chiti, Ana Rey, Jurij Diaci, Aleksi Lehtonen, Helga Pülzl, Andreas Schindlbacher, and Miguel A. Zavala · Working paper · Replication code to be made accessible upon publication






NoteAbstract





A forest carbon credit certifies one tonne of CO₂ kept from the atmosphere. After verification, three channels erode credited carbon: market leakage, finite storage duration and reversal risk. We calibrate each into one issuance rule across sixteen forest practices and three European biomes, propagating parameter uncertainty. Net climate value, the surviving share, is 9–57% (median 24%); five European schemes over-credit against it by 29–59%. Storage duration is the largest shortfall: schemes credit 30- and 100-year contracts identically. Genuine removals of 100 MtCO₂ yr⁻¹ would need ~112–336 Mha, up to twice the EU’s forest estate. Closing the 2030 land-sink gap with face-value credits would over-credit ~85 MtCO₂e a year, a €10–27 billion social cost. Levels depend on the permanence benchmark; rankings and every scheme’s over-crediting hold across the parameters tested. The EU’s adopted carbon-farming methodology prices only reversal risk; its forest-management methodology, in preparation, can price all three.

title: Research
text:
PhD thesis

Pricing Credibility: Supply-Side Integrity and Public Support in Nature Markets
AgroParisTech · submitted November 2026 · defence 10 December 2026, Nancy
Forests take up carbon and shelter most land species, so they matter for climate and biodiversity alike. In the EU most forest is private, and its carbon and habitat benefit mostly others, so owners may provide less of them than society wants. One way to close this gap is to pay owners, through public programmes or carbon credits sold to firms. Their worth depends on how much society values what they fund and on how much carbon a paid-for tonne delivers. In Austria and France, about three in four households support such programmes and would pay most for climate-adapted mixed forests. In French pilot surveys, households slightly preferred a tonne stored by a public body to one stored by a private firm. After verification, cutting avoided in one forest can move elsewhere, storage can end, and fire can release the carbon. Once these losses are deducted, 9 to 57 per cent of a verified tonne can be credited, and five European schemes deduct only part of them.

title: Oliver Frings
text:
About
I study whether nature markets deliver what they promise. On the demand side, I measure public support for forest conservation and carbon offsetting across Europe with discrete choice experiments. On the supply side, I use actuarial models and Monte Carlo simulation to price what a carbon credit delivers net of leakage, storage duration, and reversal risk.
